title: The Decision Framework — Which Mechanism, When

questions.prompt: Five independent fixes, all in one repository, and no plan to split the files between them. A colleague proposes agent teams. What is the blocking problem?
options: Agent teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees, so the five writers collide unless you partition the work by file ownership
Agent teams cannot share a task list, so nobody knows which fix is in progress
Agent teams run in the cloud, so they cannot reach files on this machine
Agent teams are limited to three peers, so five fixes do not fit
questions.explanation: The docs are explicit that agent teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees, which makes partitioning your responsibility — and the schema-less version of this task fails on exactly that. The shared-task-list answer inverts a real feature: a team's task list is one of the two things that makes it a team. Teams run where you enable them rather than in the cloud, and there is no three-peer limit in the material this lesson covers.

questions.prompt: You need the same transformation applied across 400 files, with the results collected and one summary at the end. Who should hold the plan?
options: A script — a dynamic workflow, with intermediates in script variables
Claude, turn by turn, delegating to subagents
A lead agent supervising peers
You, via agent view
questions.explanation: One repeated step across a large list is the case where the plan should be code: the script holds the list and the results, and your conversation holds the final answer. The subagents answer is the one most people reach for because it works — up to the point where the hundredth summary lands in the window and compaction turns the plan into a summary of a plan. A lead agent adds coordination you do not need for one uniform step, and handing 400 items yourself is not a plan.

questions.prompt: You have five unrelated tasks and want to hand them off, then check on them from one place without any of them living in your current conversation. Which mechanism?
options: Agent view — dispatch background sessions and watch their state
Subagents — delegate from the current conversation
Agent teams — a lead assigns the five tasks to peers
Dynamic workflows — one script spawns five agents
questions.explanation: The 'not in your conversation' clause is the discriminator: agent view exists precisely to dispatch sessions you run and check back on. Subagents are the reflex answer and they fail the clause — their results come back into your window. A team adds a lead and peer messaging you did not ask for, and a workflow's five agents return one result to a script rather than five states you can inspect and steer.

questions.prompt: Which situation actually justifies agent teams rather than a simpler mechanism?
options: Workers need to message each other directly and share a task list of who is doing what
Workers need to report results back to the conversation that spawned them
Workers need to be prevented from editing the same file
Workers need to run on a schedule
questions.explanation: Peer-to-peer messaging plus a shared task list is what a team is *for*, and it is the one thing none of the cheaper mechanisms provide. Reporting results upward is the definition of a subagent, so that option argues against a team. Preventing collisions is what worktrees do — and a team will not do it for you, which makes that option doubly wrong. Scheduling is a different family entirely.

questions.prompt: Where do loops and hooks belong in a decision about running multiple agents?
options: Outside it — they answer when something runs and what happens on an event, not how work is split
They are two more ways to run agents in parallel, alongside subagents and workflows
They are support tools, like worktrees and `/batch`
They replace the need to choose a mechanism, since a loop can dispatch agents
questions.explanation: Loops and hooks are different families: timing and event reaction. Treating them as parallelism mechanisms is how a loop gets used as a scheduler and a hook gets used as a queue. They are not support tools either — worktrees, messaging, and `/batch` exist to serve parallelism, while a loop or a hook is useful with no parallelism anywhere in sight. And a loop that dispatches agents still leaves the 'who holds the plan' question unanswered.

questions.prompt: You are choosing between a dynamic workflow and agent teams for a job that both could do. Which fact should change your plan today, before any measurement?
options: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default, and workflows need a paid plan — so availability and stability, not capability, may decide it
Agent teams are faster because peer messaging avoids the model's context window
Workflows are limited to ten agents, so a large job rules them out
Agent teams cannot use worktrees, so a workflow is always the safer choice
questions.explanation: Maturity and availability are part of the decision: an experimental feature that is off by default is not a foundation for a team process yet, and workflows require a paid plan with API access. The speed claim invents a performance characteristic the docs do not describe. Workflows scale to hundreds of agents rather than ten, so the third option gets the direction wrong — and the last option over-generalises a true fact (teams do not isolate) into a rule that ignores every other trade-off.
